Students will explore concepts about the game, different use cases for different characters, how to combine tactics to beat difficult levels and succeed in unknown ones, and, of course, experience the wonder of game design that is Arknights.
98-406 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Learn To Knit
Fall and Spring: 3 units
This beginner-friendly knitting course will teach you fundamental techniques to design and create your own garment. The course covers materials, knitting terminology, gauge swatching, and scaling your swatches. The basic skills and techniques taught in the course are designed to prepare you for your midterm and final projects. The midterm will require you to develop a design plan for a garment of your choice. The final project will be the execution of that plan. Through class sessions and homework assignments, you will gain familiarity with knitting. Class sessions will take the form of informational sessions on knitting techniques, demonstrations, and time for students to complete independent work. Yes, some days you will come to class to simply knit in a group!
98-407 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Storytime: I Survived the Internet Drama
Fall and Spring: 3 units
The world has become more virtual, and we are constantly surrounded by online news. In this course, students will learn about various moments of Internet drama, primarily controversies around popular online figures, such as Shane Dawson, Miranda Sings, and Mr. Beast. Students will also learn how to engage in online discourse, develop their own opinions, and assess opposing viewpoints. To achieve this, students will provide a creative case study and participate in a Model UN-style debate to defend their perspective.
98-408 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Philosophy in Pop Culture
Fall and Spring: 3 units
Philosophy is often seen as a purely academic subject, precluding many from participating in it. But what if it didn't have to be like that? This course will examine traditional philosophical ideas, but through the lens of pop culture institutions we usually interact with casually. How should we theorize about the future... while watching Black Mirror? What constitutes a useful ethical framework... as seen in Futurama? How sure should we be of our religious beliefs... as examined through The Good Place? You will leave this course more knowledgeable about philosophy, but critically, more aware of the philosophical implications in the world around you, even in the places you'd never expect it.
98-409 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Introduction to Rhythm Games
Fall and Spring: 3 units
This course will serve as a both comprehensive and flexible introduction to rhythm games. Throughout the course, you will be exposed to more and more different rhythm games. As you play more and more, you could build your own skills in a wide variety of games, while learning to analyze and appreciate charts (“levels”) and the structure and artistry behind them. After we cover the basics of charting and the usage of charting tools, you will craft your own chart for the game you love the most! While class time will only be an hour a week, homework is emphasized as the most important learning time for students, as it allows you to both hone their skills and allow for exploration/exposure to more charts. By the end of the course, you will have the general skills to play a variety of games, understand charts on a deeper level, and be able to create original charts. This course has no prerequisites, just be interested and have fun!
98-486 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): The Business of Sports
Fall and Spring: 3 units
The Business of Sports explores how modern sports organizations operate at the intersection of performance and profit. The course covers fundamentals of managing sports clubs under budget constraints, the role of analytics, and key economic concepts such as diminishing marginal returns. Through cases like Moneyball, Formula 1, and the failed European Super League, students will analyze trade-offs between profitability and sporting essence. The course also expands globally, studying strategies in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and China, while addressing contracts, sponsorships, and multi-club ownership. A structured debate and guest lecture capstone the course, alongside a final project where students design strategic plans for real-world clubs.
98-487 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Intro to Adobe After Effects
Fall and Spring: 3 units
Intro to Adobe After Effects is a beginner-friendly course that provides a comprehensive overview of motion graphics and visual effects. Students will learn interface and workflow basics, keyframe animation, text and shape animation, compositing, and rendering. Through hands-on projects, they will create dynamic animated videos and build their first portfolio pieces. The midterm challenges students to produce a 20–30 second animated explainer video, while the final project allows them to design a polished, creative motion graphics piece of their choice. By the end of the course, students will be able to confidently use After Effects to create professional-quality animations for presentations, branding, and storytelling.
98-488 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): The Language of Hands: ASL Foundations
Fall and Spring: 3 units
An interactive beginner-level course in American Sign Language (ASL) that introduces basic vocabulary, fingerspelling, grammar, facial expressions, and classifiers, while also engaging with Deaf culture and history. Students will complete weekly video homework to practice expressive and receptive skills, participate in peer-to-peer activities, and gain cultural awareness. A midterm expressive/receptive assessment and a creative ASL video project serve as the main evaluations. No prior ASL knowledge required.
98-489 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Decoding Hidden Messages in Media
Fall and Spring: 3 units
This interactive course explores how creators hide secret codes, easter eggs, and ciphers across media such as video games, cartoons, and web series. Students learn to decode text ciphers (Caesar, Atbash, Vigen and #232;re), image manipulations, and audio distortions. Assignments include weekly decoding tasks, a midterm in-class exam, and a final project analyzing a coded video. By the end of the course, students will be able to independently recognize and decode hidden messages.
98-501 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): The Art and Science of Origami
Fall and Spring: 3 units
Origami, far more than “the ancient Japanese art of paperfolding,” is a very modern art form with many technical and artistic advancements achieved in the last few decades. Despite this, most of the capabilities of modern origami remain unknown to the larger public. This class will serve as an introduction to how origami is practiced in the modern day: on the one hand, the technical aspects of how origami bases are created; on the other hand, the artistic aspects of how those bases are shaped into finished models. The aim of the class is to display origami as it truly is: modern, international, equal parts art and science.
98-502 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Introduction to Writing Dystopian Fiction
Fall and Spring: 3 units
"The beauty of dystopia is that it lets us vicariously experience future worlds - because we still have the power to change our own." - Ally Condie This course is a genre fiction writing class. We will learn how to write effective stories in the dystopian genre, by exploring themes and tropes in dystopian media and learning how to employ them in our own writing. The study of dystopias will be approached through four units: theme, worldbuilding, character, and plot. Classes will be a mix of lecture and discussion, with time for workshopping student work towards the end of the semester. Activities will include: Discussing and learning about the dystopian genre Reading examples of dystopian fiction Exercises and assignments in creative writing Workshopping each other’s work Students will leave the course with an original plan for a Dystopian story. Aside from being super fun, dystopias reflect aspects of our own society and provide space for contemplation, and their study makes us more informed and conscientious people.
98-503 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Jurassic Park: Science, Ethics, and Cinema
Fall and Spring: 3 units
This course explores Jurassic Park (1993), The Lost World: Jurassic Park (1997), and Jurassic Park III (2001) as both scientific cautionary tales and blockbuster filmmaking achievements. Through an interdisciplinary lens, we will examine the ethical implications of genetic engineering, the portrayal of science and technology in film, and the evolution of the franchise’s storytelling, themes, and cultural impact.
98-504 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Introduction to Tennis Analytics
Fall and Spring: 3 units
This course introduces students to fundamental topics in analysis of tennis at a competitive level and prepares students with simple statistical techniques for studying the game. We will begin the course by discussing how analytical data is collected in the modern game. Next, we transition to discussing how an individual match is measured, including service statistics, return statistics, net statistics, performance by rally length, and W/UFE ratio. In the second half of this course, we extend these analytical techniques to study player performance over multiple matches and consider larger trends such as surface, tournament level, performance against top 5/10/15, and other more general topics.
98-505 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Mindful Crafting: Relaxation in the Digital Age
Fall and Spring: 3 units
In a hyper-connected digital world, crafting has emerged as both an online and offline practice that fosters mindfulness, creativity, and community. From diamond painting to digital scrapbooking, this course explores how crafting—both physical and virtual—enhances focus, reduces stress, and cultivates mindfulness. Students will engage in hands-on crafting, explore digital crafting communities (YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Reddit, etc.), and study the psychology behind creative flow states through hands-on projects and in-class discussions. By the end of the course, students will develop their own mindful craft project. Course fee $5
98-506 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Introduction to Web Development
Fall and Spring: 3 units
Students will learn the syntax, usage, and applications of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to create webpages. Students will become familiar with the process of creating and implementing a website from the ground up. The importance of creating semantically correct, well-structured, and accessible HTML will be emphasized. The core concepts of CSS will be covered, including selectors, specificity, the box model, grid/flex, and the importance of CSS in creating a responsive website. Topics of JavaScript that will be covered include accessing the DOM, event handlers, async/await, and various browser APIs such as fetch, localStorage, History, and more. As a part of the course, students will progressively work to create a fully-fledged website of their choice, which serves as a final project. Familiarity with programming concepts at the level of 15-110 is recommended, but no background knowledge in any one specific language is necessary. We welcome all those interested in web development to give this course a try!
98-507 Student Taught Courses (StuCo): Music in Motion
Fall and Spring: 3 units
Do you tap your foot when you listen to music? Have you ever thought of something as groovy but can't explain why? Do you find yourself wishing you could improve your rhythmic or musical abilities? Well that's great if you have, and completely fine if you haven't. Music in Motion is a class based around the Eurhythmics style of teaching, which helps students make deeper connections with the music they listen to and interact with. As a movement-based class, this class allows you to internalize the music and "feel the feels" by moving your body and learning kinesthetically. In each class, students will engage with music, either live or recorded, in various group settings that will invite them to view music differently and engage actively with their peers. Music in Motion is a class environment that encourages play, allows for mistakes, and invites students to make choices about how they interact with the space and people around them.
